examples.note: This demonstrates an explicitly historical reference, not use of an obsolete name as current.

parts.quote: The Democratic Republic of the Congo used to be called ‘Zaire’. The former name came from the Portuguese colonial name for the Congo River.

rules.quote: Refer to peoples and places outside Australia based on current information.
rules.specification: Check the currency of names and geographic descriptions, not whether the writer performed research. An explicitly historical reference to a former name is not a claim that it is current.
rules.violation_condition: A reference to a people or place outside Australia presents outdated naming or geographic information as current.
when: When referring to the current name or status of a people or place outside Australia.
Historical names may appear in references explicitly presented as historical.
rules.why: G-5 distinguishes a checkable property of the reference—currency—from advice about researching it.

examples.note: Explaining a full name and its short form is not inconsistent ordinary reference.

parts.quote: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is often called the ‘United Kingdom’.

rules.specification: Check for a stable naming convention among alternative country names. Introducing a full name and its clear, accurate short form, or explaining alternative names, is not itself inconsistent usage.
rules.violation_condition: A document inconsistently switches between alternative names for the same country.
when: When a country has alternative names and a name has been selected for use.
Assess ordinary references, rather than passages explaining alternative or historical names.
rules.why: G-5 excludes the research instruction while retaining the independently checkable requirement for consistent naming.

covers.quote: Use initial capitals for:
the official name of a country
any commonly used short forms of the country’s name
the names of states, territories and provinces.
When the name is used generically, you don’t need an initial capital.

examples.note: Official names and their short forms retain initial capitals.

rules.quote: Spell country names with a capital letter
rules.violation_condition: An official country name, a commonly used short form, or a state, territory or province name lacks its required initial capitals.
when: Applies to official country names, commonly used short forms, and names of states, territories and provinces.
An initial capital is not required when a name is used generically.
The definite article ‘the’ is governed by the separate article-capitalisation rule.
rules.why: G-2 combines the listed name categories and the generic-use exception; G-4 absorbs the body's restatement.

examples.note: The article remains lower case while the names take capitals.

rules.quote: The definite article ‘the’ isn’t capitalised unless it begins a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: The definite article before a country or place name is written as ‘The’ when it does not begin a sentence.
when: When ‘the’ precedes a country or place name.
A capital is appropriate when the article begins a sentence.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the sentence-initial exception with the article check; this is distinct from capitalising the name itself.

covers.quote: Shorten a country name only if it is clear to the user

examples.note: The shortened form identifies the same country accurately.

parts.quote: ‘North Korea’ is the shortened form of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

rules.quote: Use a short form of a country’s name only if it’s clear and accurate.
rules.specification: Assess clarity using the intended audience and the document's context, including any earlier introduction of the name. Accuracy requires the short form to identify the intended country rather than a different or broader entity.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened country name is ambiguous to the intended user or inaccurately identifies the country.
when: When a shortened country name is used.
rules.why: G-4 selects the body wording because it includes both clarity and accuracy; these are conditions on the same shortening check.

covers.quote: English-language content usually uses the English version of a country’s name.
There are some cases where the preferred official name isn’t in English.
In English-speaking countries, the convention is to use the established English forms for well-known place names.

examples.note: These illustrate English versions; the foreign names mentioned for comparison are not presented as errors.

parts.quote: ‘Socialist Republic of Vietnam’ is the English version of Cộng hòa xã hội chủ nghĩa Việt Nam.
‘Germany’ is the English version of Deutschland.
‘New Zealand’ is the English version of Aotearoa.
‘The Czech Republic’ or ‘Czechia’ are the English versions of Česká republika.

examples.note: Preferred official names illustrate exceptions to the English-form convention.

parts.quote: ‘Côte d’Ivoire’ is the preferred official name for the Ivory Coast.
‘Eswatini’ is the preferred name for Swaziland.

examples.note: These illustrate established English place-name forms.

rules.quote: Use English versions of countries and places in most content
rules.specification: Interpret the heading through the body: apply it to English-language content and, for places, to names with established English forms. Preferred official non-English names are exceptions. Do not assume every unfamiliar place name has an English alternative.
rules.violation_condition: English-language content uses a non-English country name or a non-English form of a well-known place name where an established English form is expected and no preferred-official-name exception applies.
when: In English-language content.
For place names, when the place is well known and has an established English form.
A preferred official name may be non-English; the page gives Côte d’Ivoire and Eswatini.
rules.why: G-2 combines country and place-name cases with the preferred-name exception; G-4 avoids separate findings for the body restatements.

covers.quote: Some names that aren’t officially recognised become well known and gain a semi-official status.

examples.note: Recognised regional names take initial capitals.
This illustrates a well-known name with semi-official status.

rules.quote: Groups of nations or areas that are recognised as political or geographic regions take initial capitals.
rules.violation_condition: The name of a recognised political or geographic region lacks its required initial capitals.
when: For names of groups of nations or areas recognised as political or geographic regions.
Recognition can include well-known names that have gained semi-official status.
An initial capital is not required when a name is used generically.
rules.why: G-2 retains recognition and semi-official status as cases of one regional-name capitalisation check; G-5 excludes the research advice.

examples.note: The directional terms describe areas rather than forming part of the names.

rules.quote: Use lower case if the names of compass points (such as north and south-east) are not part of the name but are used to refer to the geographic area.
rules.violation_condition: A compass-point or directional term is capitalised away from the start of a sentence even though it describes a geographic area rather than forming part of its name.
when: When a compass point or directional term describes an area rather than forming part of a proper name.
Do not flag a capital required at the beginning of a sentence.
rules.why: G-2 keeps proper-name membership as the condition on one lower-case check, distinct from capitalising recognised regional names.

covers.quote: Capitalise the names of certain groups.
When the name is used generically, you don’t need an initial capital.

examples.note: The nationality terms take initial capitals.
These identify the group-name cases covered by the capitalisation check.

parts.quote: People groups – Hispanic, Sentinelese, Vietnamese Rục, Sámi
People from particular regions – Asian, European, Sumatran, Basque
People who follow particular religions – Jewish, Christian, Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu, Greek Orthodox
People who speak particular languages – Hokkien-speaking

examples.note: Generic uses are exempt from the initial-capital requirement; these are not evidence that capitals are prohibited.

rules.quote: Write nationalities, peoples and places with initial capitals
rules.violation_condition: A nationality term or the name of a people or group lacks its required initial capitals.
when: This entry covers nationality terms and names of peoples and groups; geographic place names are assigned to the more specific country- and region-name rules.
The illustrated groups include people groups, clans, people from particular regions, religious groups and language groups.
An initial capital is not required when a name is used generically.
rules.why: G-2 combines the nationality and group-name cases; G-4 absorbs the body restatement, while more specific place-name rules prevent duplicate findings.
